analysis.one_liner: Creates free emergency insulin cards for uninsured people and taxes insulin makers that spike prices.
analysis.headline: The insulin assistance bill, introduced with one cosponsor in May 2023, never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send grants to states, tribes, and tribal organizations to run "insulin card" programs giving uninsured and underinsured people insulin at no cost at pharmacies. It pays for the program by charging insulin makers an annual fee based on their market share, and it adds an excise tax — up to 100% of the extra revenue — on manufacturers that raise insulin prices faster than inflation. It would also shorten the period during which brand-name biologic drug makers are shielded from cheaper copycat versions, from 12 years to 7.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people and people in high-deductible health plans who need insulin: they could get an initial roughly 7-day supply within 5 business days of applying, then renewable 90-day supplies at no cost [S3]. Payments made on behalf of underinsured enrollees would count toward their plan deductible, so they would not lose that money [S2, S3]. States, tribes, and tribal health programs would get federal funding and a new tool to stop insulin rationing among residents they serve [S3]. Pharmacies would be paid to dispense the insulin [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured people who need insulin

how_it_helps.text: Grants to states, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations would fund insulin card programs that let uninsured or underinsured people get insulin at pharmacies at no cost — an initial roughly 7-day supply within 5 business days of applying, then a renewable 90-day card

For people in high-deductible health plans, amounts the program pays pharmacies for their insulin must count toward their deductible and other out-of-pocket requirements, so they are not charged twice for the same medicine
The program is funded by annual fees on insulin manufacturers, apportioned by each company's share of insulin sales, equal to the program's total cost from 2024 through 2028

An excise tax would hit manufacturers whose insulin prices rise faster than the inflation index: 50% of the extra revenue for smaller spikes, 75% for spikes of 15–20%, and 100% for spikes of 20% or more, with an exemption process for genuine cost-driven increases
The bill shortens market exclusivity for biological drugs from 12 years to 7, which would let cheaper biosimilar competitors reach the market years sooner

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would pay annual fees covering the full cost of the grant program and would owe excise taxes on price-spike revenue, while all biologic drug makers — not just insulin makers — would lose 5 years of market exclusivity under the bill's shortest provision [S2, S3]. States, tribes, and tribal organizations would have to contribute at least $1 of their own for every $3 in federal grant money, and the Treasury would deposit the fees in the general fund [S3].

drawbacks.text: The grant program sunsets after 5 years, so it is an emergency bridge rather than a lasting fix for insulin affordability
It covers only uninsured people and people in high-deductible plans; insured people whose plans impose insulin copays get no relief
States, tribes, and tribal organizations must put up at least $1 in non-federal matching funds for every $3 of federal money, which could keep poorer states and tribes from participating
The exclusivity cut from 12 to 7 years applies to all biological drugs, not only insulin, which industry argues would reduce the incentive to develop new biologic medicines across the board

The tiered price-spike tax penalizes any increase above the annual inflation allowance, which could push manufacturers toward repeated increases right at the inflation ceiling rather than holding prices steady

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is sound: the people who most often ration insulin — the uninsured and those in high-deductible plans — get immediate free access, and the program is fully funded by the companies selling the product rather than by taxpayers. The honest costs are that it is a five-year stopgap that leaves most insured people's insulin costs untouched, requires a state match that may exclude poorer jurisdictions, and reaches beyond insulin by cutting exclusivity for every biologic drug, the provision most likely to draw an industry challenge that the bill never faced because it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and a health subcommittee for about 20 months and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on May 9, 2023, joined by Rep. Dean Phillips as its only cosponsor
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees the day it was introduced, splitting it between jurisdictions that each had to act separately
On May 12, 2023 it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where no markup or vote followed
On December 17, 2024 — more than 19 months later and less than three weeks before the Congress ended — it was re-referred to the same subcommittee, still without any hearing or vote on record
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving the program, fees, price-spike tax, and exclusivity cut unenacted

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin and biologic drug manufacturers are better off: they kept the full 12-year exclusivity period, faced no new annual fees, no price-spike excise tax, and no quarterly price reporting. Uninsured and underinsured people who ration insulin gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its insulin card program, manufacturer fees, price-spike tax, and exclusivity cut

for.name: Rep. Dean Phillips
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, which sat in her committee and then its Health Subcommittee from May 2023 until the Congress ended

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill, which covered the tax and fee provisions within his committee's jurisdiction

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so no roll-call split exists; both sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-controlled committees never moved the bill, while no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill charges them an annual fee covering the full cost of the free-insulin program, imposes quarterly price reporting, and taxes up to 100% of revenue from price increases above inflation. The record does not show their position, but the fees and tax come directly out of their revenue.

industries.industry: Biologic drug makers (all biotech and large pharma)
industries.note: Shortening exclusivity from 12 to 7 years applies to every biological drug, not just insulin, letting biosimilar competitors reach the market years earlier. This hits the entire brand-name biotech industry's patent-protected pricing window.
States would contract with pharmacies to dispense free insulin to card holders and pay them for it, bringing in sales they otherwise might not make from uninsured customers.

They must credit program payments toward enrollees' deductibles, slightly reducing how much deductible spending their customers absorb, in exchange for a healthier, less rationing-prone risk pool and modest reporting duties.
